title: US Midterms on November 3 Will Shape H-1B, Green Card Debate
excerpt: Control of Congress will decide whether H-1B and green card bills can move, while the $100,000 fee and PERM suspensions already in force rest with the executive branch
body:
• US midterm elections are on November 3, 2026; the party that controls Congress will decide whether bills to change H-1B rules, per-country green card caps or fees can pass, while executive orders already in force do not need Congress.
  • The $100,000 H-1B payment already applies to certain petitions filed on or after September 21, 2025 for beneficiaries outside the US without a valid H-1B visa; it does not apply to previously issued, currently valid H-1B visas, per USCIS.
  • The Labour Department has suspended PERM green card certifications for eight technology companies, according to midterm coverage; workers at those firms who have not started PERM cannot begin employer sponsorship until it resumes.
  • Green card waits will not be reset by the election alone: the November 2026 Visa Bulletin keeps India's EB-2 final action date at November 1, 2013 and EB-3 at January 22, 2014.

The US midterm elections on November 3 will not rewrite immigration law on their own, but they will decide who controls the committees and floor votes that any change to H-1B visas or employment-based green cards must pass through. For Indian professionals, who receive the largest share of H-1B visas and face the longest green card queues, the result sets what is politically possible for the next two years.

What Congress controls, and what it does not

The core rules are statutory: the H-1B programme's structure, annual employment-based green card limits and the per-country caps behind India's backlog can only be changed by legislation. Either party's Congress can block or advance such bills, and committee chairs decide which proposals get hearings.

Much of the current pressure on Indian workers, however, comes from executive action, which continues regardless of the midterm result unless Congress legislates or courts intervene. USCIS states that under the presidential proclamation of September 19, 2025, certain H-1B petitions filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on September 21, 2025 must include an additional $100,000 payment, applying to beneficiaries outside the United States who do not hold a valid H-1B visa. USCIS also states the proclamation does not apply to previously issued and currently valid H-1B visas or to petitions submitted before that deadline, and does not prevent current H-1B holders from travelling in and out of the United States.

Separately, BizzBuzz and NationPress report that the Labour Department has suspended PERM labour certifications, the first step in employer-sponsored green cards, for eight technology companies. That too is executive action; a new Congress could pressure the administration through oversight and funding, but cannot lift it by vote alone.

The campaign squeeze on Indian-American candidates

The election has put Indian-American candidates under pressure from both parties. At least nine Indian Americans are on the November 3 ballot as Republicans, according to community media tallies, led by Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor and including Saritha Komatireddy, nominee for New York attorney general, three US House nominees and state candidates in New York, Tennessee, California and Michigan. They are campaigning while the Trump administration takes a harder line on skilled immigration, in a programme dominated by Indian professionals.

On the Democratic side, the pressure arrived in primaries. Representative Shri Thanedar lost Michigan's August 4 primary to Donavan McKinney, 51.9 percent to 48.1 percent. Assemblywoman Jenifer Rajkumar lost New York's June 23 primary to David Orkin, 58.8 percent to 40.9 percent, and Rahul Garabadu lost a June 16 Georgia runoff to Ruwa Romman, 60.1 percent to 39.9 percent. Two Democrats remain in competitive races: Los Angeles Councilmember Nithya Raman led Mayor Karen Bass 39 percent to 28 percent in a September 15-20 Berkeley IGS poll, and Texas candidate Pooja Sethi could become the first Indian American in the Texas Legislature if she wins on November 3.

The backlog the election will not clear

Even a favourable result leaves the green card queue unchanged. The State Department's November 2026 Visa Bulletin keeps India's EB-2 final action date at November 1, 2013 and advances EB-3 only to January 22, 2014, while most other countries stand at April 1, 2025 in EB-2. Only Congress can raise the per-country limits behind that gap, which is why immigration lawyers treat midterm control of the House and Senate as the precondition for any backlog bill, rather than as relief itself.

What Indian applicants should do now

Three practical points hold whichever party wins. First, existing status is not changed by the election: valid H-1B visas remain valid, and the $100,000 payment, where it applies, turns on filing date and the beneficiary's location, not November 3. Second, workers whose employers have not started PERM should confirm whether their employer is among the firms affected by the reported suspension. Third, applicants with priority dates near the Visa Bulletin cutoffs should keep documents ready, because filing windows can open with a month's notice.
